steps.title: Check how many logons failed and from which source IPs
steps.help: Open the related events. One source IP hitting one user is classic guessing; many IPs can mean a password spray.

steps.title: Check whether any logon succeeded after the failures
steps.help: Search Event ID 4624 for the same user just after the failures. A success after many failures is the dangerous case.

steps.title: Contact the user to confirm whether it was them
steps.help: Typing a password wrong a few times after a password change is the most common benign cause.

steps.title: Lock or reset the account if it was not the user
steps.help: Containment: stop the attacker from using a guessed password.

steps.title: Block the source IP at the firewall if it is external
steps.help: Only for addresses outside the company network.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Write what you checked and why you chose the verdict.

steps.title: Identify who created or changed the account
steps.help: The 'user' field on the 4720/4732 event is the account that made the change.

steps.title: Look for a matching change ticket or request
steps.help: Approved admin work should have a ticket. No ticket is a red flag.

steps.title: Check what the new account has done since
steps.help: Search Log Search for the new account name (target user) to see logons and actions.

steps.title: Disable the account if it is not authorised
steps.help: Containment: remove access before investigating further.

steps.title: Review membership of admin groups
steps.help: Make sure no other unexpected accounts were added at the same time.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Record the ticket number, or why the change was not approved.

steps.title: Check the user's normal working hours and role
steps.help: Some staff (admins, on-call) work at night as part of the job.

steps.title: Check for planned maintenance at that time
steps.help: Patching windows often happen in the early morning.

steps.title: Confirm with the user or their manager
steps.help: Ask in a way that does not tip off an attacker using the account, e.g. by phone.

steps.title: Review what happened after the logon
steps.help: Look for account changes, unusual connections or EDR detections on the same host.

steps.title: Reset the credentials if the logon is not confirmed
steps.help: Containment for possibly stolen credentials.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Planned work with a ticket is usually 'benign'.

name: Connection to known-bad IP or domain (beacon)

steps.title: Look up the indicator in the threat-intel list
steps.help: Generator tab shows the fake intel list and what each entry means.

steps.title: Identify the host and process making the connection
steps.help: Check firewall/DNS events and any EDR events on that host.

steps.title: Check whether other hosts contacted the same indicator
steps.help: Search Log Search by the IP or domain with no host filter.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host from the network
steps.help: Containment: stop it talking to the attacker's controller.

steps.title: Block the indicator at the firewall and DNS
steps.help: Prevents other hosts from reaching it.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Repeated connections at regular intervals point to beaconing.

steps.title: Review the EDR detection details
steps.help: Note the host, user and the generic tool description.

steps.title: Check whether the tool was blocked or ran
steps.help: A blocked tool is less urgent than one that ran, but still needs follow-up.

steps.title: Isolate the host
steps.help: Containment: a credential theft tool means passwords on that host may be exposed.

steps.title: Reset credentials of accounts that used the host
steps.help: Assume any password typed on the host is known to the attacker.

steps.title: Escalate to an incident case
steps.help: Use 'Escalate to case' so the wider investigation has one timeline.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Write down which accounts were reset.

steps.title: Read the delivered email: sender, SPF result, subject and recipient count
steps.help: Search Log Search with source "mail" and the user. A failed SPF check, an urgent password subject and only one or two recipients point to targeted phishing. A newsletter goes to many people and passes SPF.

steps.title: Check what happened after the click
steps.help: Look for DNS and firewall events from the user's PC to the link's domain and IP, and for a form_submit event (the user typed credentials into the page).

steps.title: Look for logons from new IPs after the click
steps.help: Search the user in Log Search with event ID 4624. A successful logon from a 203.0.113.x address the user has never used before means the stolen password is being used. No rule alerts on it: you have to look.

steps.title: Reset the password and end the user's sessions if credentials were entered
steps.help: Containment: the attacker's copy of the password stops working.

steps.title: Block the domain and purge the email from every mailbox
steps.help: Other people may have received the same email. Add the domain and IP to the intel list.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: A legitimate newsletter on a new domain is benign; a lookalike page asking for a password is a true positive.

steps.title: List the accounts the source IP tried
steps.help: Open the related events. Spraying is one IP, many users, one or two attempts each.

steps.title: Check whether any of those accounts logged on successfully from the same IP
steps.help: Search the source IP in Log Search for Event ID 4624. One success means one account is in the attacker's hands.

steps.title: Reset any account that logged on from the IP
steps.help: Containment: assume the guessed password is known.

steps.title: Block the source IP at the firewall
steps.help: It is external (203.0.113.x). Also add it to the intel list.

steps.title: Check whether the tried accounts share a weak password policy
steps.help: Spraying works against common passwords. This is the lesson-learned for the post-incident review.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: List the accounts tried and whether any succeeded.

steps.title: Identify the account, the source PC and the PCs it logged on to
steps.help: Open the related events. Is the source the user's own PC?

steps.title: Check the user's role
steps.help: IT admins do remote work on PCs; other staff almost never log on to someone else's PC over the network.

steps.title: Look for an approved change ticket in the change log
steps.help: Search Log Search with source "change". A ticket that lists exactly these hosts and covers this time means planned work.

steps.title: Isolate the source PC and reset the account if there is no ticket
steps.help: Containment: stop the spread and cut off the stolen credentials.

steps.title: Review what the account did on each target PC
steps.help: Search each target host for EDR detections, new accounts or unusual connections.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Record the change reference if the work was planned.

name: Beacon pattern to an unknown address

steps.title: Confirm the pattern: same host, same IP, regular intervals
steps.help: Open the related events and look at the times. Software checking in on a timer is the sign of a beacon.

steps.title: Look up the IP in IOC Lookup
steps.help: It may be on no intel list. That does not make it safe: the behaviour is the evidence.

steps.title: Check whether other hosts talk to the same IP
steps.help: Search the IP in Log Search with no host filter.

steps.title: Isolate the host
steps.help: Containment: stop it talking to the controller.

steps.title: Add the IP to the intel list and block it
steps.help: From now on the known-bad IP rule (R005) also catches it.

steps.title: Document the findings and set a verdict
steps.help: Note the interval and how long the beaconing went on.

name: Successful logon from an internet address

steps.title: Confirm the source address is outside the company
steps.help: Company hosts use 192.0.2.x. A 203.0.113.x source is the simulated internet, so this logon came from outside.

steps.title: Check which account, which host and how it logged on
steps.help: Logon type 10 is Remote Desktop and type 3 is over the network. Note whether the host is a server and whether the account is privileged.

steps.title: Look for what led up to the logon
steps.help: Search the user in Log Search and the source IP in IOC Lookup: earlier 4625 failures (R001, R009) or a phishing click and form submit (R008) explain how the password was obtained.

steps.title: Look for what the account did after the logon
steps.help: Search the user for special-privilege logons (4672), new accounts (4720), admin group changes (4732) and logons to other hosts.

steps.title: Contain: reset the password, end the session and block the address
steps.help: Stop the attacker from using the account, and block the source IP at the firewall.

steps.title: Open a case and set a verdict
steps.help: A confirmed logon by an outsider is an account takeover. Record the timeline, the evidence and the actions taken.
